newsitem.title: USA: Panel named to keep small U.S. farmers on land.
newsitem.headline: Panel named to keep small U.S. farmers on land.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman named a 27-member commission Wednesday to try to find ways to keep small farmers on the land.
The number of farms in the United States has declined steadily since the Depression to about 2.06 million now.
Mechanization and greater productivity due to hybrid seeds, fertilisers and pesticides that allow farmers to till bigger areas in less time have played a role in the decline.
The appointment of the commission was an outgrowth of a review that found the Agriculture Department had discriminated in the past against minority farmers in its lending programmes.
In the past, there was no federal reaction to the declining number of farms, Glickman said at a news conference.
"So the question is not big vs. little, but can we find a meaningful way for the two to co-exist?" Glickman said. "I'd like to think the answer is yes."

Former congressman Harold Volkmer, a Missouri Democrat, was named as chairman of the National Commission on Small Farms. Its first meeting will be Monday in Memphis, Tenn., with a deadline to produce by Sept. 30 a national strategy to "make life a little easier for America's small farmers and ranchers," Glickman said.
The commission will look at various approaches, such as "niche" crops, direct marketing through farmers' markets and possible changes in federal or state programmes.

Members of the commission include Chuck Hassebrook of the small farm-oriented Centre for Rural Affairs, a number of farmers, agribusiness executives and members of the Ford and W.K. Kellogg foundations.
Glickman said recent changes in federal agricultural programmes under the so-called "Freedom to Farm" law carried the risk of larger swings in farmers' incomes because it reduced subsidy spending.
An overriding question, he said, would be whether the government could aid small farmers in the face of the long-term shift to fewer and larger farms.

Earl Butz, who was agriculture secretary during the Nixon administration, said in an interview that American agriculture had "pretty much made the adjustment now to putting farms in larger, more (economically) competent units."
The result, he said, was that a group of 600,000 commercial-size farms produced 80 percent of U.S. crops and livestock.
